title: How to Inspect Links Before Clicking
overview: Learn how to inspect URLs, recognise suspicious domains, and slow down before clicking links in emails or messages.
objectives: Inspect a link before clicking it
Spot lookalike domains and suspicious URL patterns
Use a simple check process before trusting login links
keyPoints: The real destination URL matters more than the button text
Unexpected login prompts should always be treated carefully
redFlags: Rushed wording pushing you to click quickly
checklist: Hover or inspect the link target
Check the root domain carefully
Ask whether the message was expected
Avoid signing in through unsolicited links

examples.title: Fake account verification email
examples.scenario: An email asks you to verify your account immediately using a button that looks genuine.
examples.takeaway: Always inspect the real destination before trusting the button.

reflectionQuestions: What clue would make you stop before clicking?
How would you verify a login request safely?

checkQuestions.prompt: What is the best first step before clicking a link in an email?

options.text: Check the real destination URL
options.feedback: Correct. The destination URL is one of the strongest phishing checks.

options.text: Trust it if the button looks professional
options.feedback: Button styling is easy to fake.

options.text: Click it first and decide after the page loads
options.feedback: That is too late. The check should happen before clicking.

checkQuestions.prompt: Which of these is the stronger phishing clue?

options.text: A message using your name
options.feedback: Personalisation is easy for attackers to fake.

options.text: A lookalike domain in the link
options.feedback: Correct. A suspicious domain is a major warning sign.

options.text: A blue sign-in button
options.feedback: Visual design tells you very little by itself.

title: Spotting Urgency and Pressure Tactics
overview: Understand how attackers use fear, urgency, and pressure to force rushed decisions.
objectives: Recognise urgency as a manipulation tactic
Slow down when a message tries to create panic
Choose a safer response instead of reacting instantly
keyPoints: Pressure is used to reduce careful thinking
Independent verification breaks the attacker’s momentum
redFlags: Threats of account closure or penalty
checklist: Pause before acting
Check whether the request is expected
Verify through a trusted channel
Do not let countdown language rush you

examples.title: Invoice due now
examples.scenario: A message says payment must be made within the hour or service will be suspended.
examples.takeaway: Urgency should make you verify the request, not obey it immediately.

reflectionQuestions: What type of message pressures you most?
How can you slow yourself down when a message feels urgent?

checkQuestions.prompt: Why do attackers use urgency in phishing messages?

options.text: To help users make informed decisions
options.feedback: Urgency is meant to reduce careful thinking, not improve it.

options.text: To pressure users into acting before checking
options.feedback: Correct. Pressure is used to force rushed decisions.

options.text: Because legitimate organisations always use threats
options.feedback: Threatening language is not proof of legitimacy.

checkQuestions.prompt: What is the safest response to a highly urgent payment email?

options.text: Pay immediately to stay safe
options.feedback: That is exactly what the attacker wants.

options.text: Forward it to everyone for advice
options.feedback: That does not verify the request safely.

options.text: Verify it through a trusted and separate channel
options.feedback: Correct. Independent verification is the safest response.

title: Attachments, Macros and Safe Opening Habits
overview: Covers risky attachments, fake invoices, and why macro-enabled files are dangerous.
objectives: Use safer habits when opening files
keyPoints: Macro prompts are a serious warning sign
Unexpected invoices and documents should be verified first
redFlags: Requests to enable macros or editing
checklist: Check whether the attachment was expected
Verify the sender and request
Do not enable macros unless fully trusted
Treat invoice attachments cautiously

examples.title: Fake invoice spreadsheet
examples.scenario: An email includes an invoice spreadsheet and tells you to enable content to view it properly.
examples.takeaway: Requests to enable content or macros are a major risk signal.

reflectionQuestions: What type of attachment would make you stop and verify first?
Why are macro prompts such a strong warning sign?

checkQuestions.prompt: What should you do if a document asks you to enable macros?

options.text: Enable them so the file works properly
options.feedback: That can activate malicious code.

options.text: Treat it as suspicious and verify before doing anything
options.feedback: Correct. Macro prompts are a major red flag.

options.text: Ignore the warning if the sender seems busy
options.feedback: Pressure from the message should not override safety checks.

checkQuestions.prompt: Which attachment scenario is more suspicious?

options.text: An expected file from a known colleague
options.feedback: This can still be risky, but it is less suspicious than an unexpected invoice.

options.text: An unexpected invoice attachment demanding urgent review
options.feedback: Correct. Unexpected invoices plus urgency are strong phishing signals.

options.text: A file sent after you requested it through a trusted channel
options.feedback: Expected files are not automatically safe, but the context is stronger.

title: Building Strong Password Habits
overview: Learn what makes a password strong, how reuse creates risk, and how to create better credentials.
objectives: Understand what makes a password stronger
See why password reuse increases risk
Build safer password habits for everyday use
keyPoints: Reused passwords spread damage across accounts
A strong password habit is more important than one perfect password
redFlags: Using the same password across services
Using very short or common passwords
checklist: Use longer passwords or passphrases
Avoid reusing passwords
Do not build passwords around obvious personal details
Store strong unique passwords safely

examples.title: Password reuse problem
examples.scenario: A breached shopping site exposes a password that is also used on email and banking accounts.
examples.takeaway: Reuse turns one breach into a much bigger problem.

reflectionQuestions: Where might you still be reusing passwords?
What small habit change would improve your password security most?

options.text: Because it makes typing slightly slower
options.feedback: That is not the real issue.

options.text: Because one breach can affect multiple accounts
options.feedback: Correct. Reuse allows one compromise to spread.

options.text: Because websites dislike repeated passwords
options.feedback: The real risk is account compromise, not preference.

options.text: A unique long password for each account
options.feedback: Correct. Uniqueness plus length is much safer.

options.text: One memorable password used everywhere
options.feedback: That creates widespread risk if it is exposed.

options.text: A short password changed every year
options.feedback: Short and predictable passwords are still weak.

title: Using a Password Manager Properly
overview: Explains what password managers do, why they help, and what good password manager behaviour looks like.
objectives: Know what a password manager should and should not be used for
keyPoints: Password managers support unique passwords at scale
The master password matters a lot
Convenience can improve security when used properly
redFlags: Saving sensitive passwords in insecure notes
Avoiding password managers due to myths
checklist: Use a strong master password
Store account passwords in the manager instead of reusing them
Review saved credentials periodically
Do not share your manager access casually

examples.title: From reuse to unique passwords
examples.scenario: A user replaces reused passwords with unique generated ones stored in a password manager.
examples.takeaway: Password managers make strong unique credentials much more practical.

reflectionQuestions: What has stopped you from using a password manager fully?
How would a manager reduce your reuse risk?

checkQuestions.prompt: What is one of the main benefits of a password manager?

options.text: It encourages password reuse
options.feedback: It should reduce reuse, not encourage it.

options.text: It makes unique passwords easier to manage
options.feedback: Correct. That is one of its biggest security benefits.

options.text: It removes the need for any security habits
options.feedback: A password manager helps, but it does not replace good habits.

checkQuestions.prompt: What should be especially strong when using a password manager?

options.text: The master password
options.feedback: Correct. The master password protects access to the vault.

options.text: Only your least important account password
options.feedback: The master password is the critical one here.

options.text: The website colour theme
options.feedback: That has nothing to do with credential security.

title: Social Engineering Fundamentals
overview: Covers impersonation, authority abuse, urgency tactics, and how attackers manipulate trust.
objectives: Understand how social engineering manipulates trust
Respond more carefully when human pressure is used
keyPoints: Attackers target judgement as much as technology
Authority, urgency and familiarity are common manipulation tools
A separate verification step reduces risk
redFlags: Mismatch between claimed identity and message details
checklist: Pause before complying
Check whether the identity claim makes sense
Verify through another channel
Do not rely only on tone or familiarity

examples.title: Fake senior leader request
examples.scenario: A message claims to be from a senior leader and asks for urgent action outside normal process.
examples.takeaway: Authority claims should be verified, especially when they bypass normal checks.

reflectionQuestions: Which influence tactic affects you most: authority, urgency or familiarity?
What independent check would you use before responding?

checkQuestions.prompt: What is social engineering mainly trying to exploit?

options.text: Human judgement and behaviour
options.feedback: Correct. Social engineering attacks people and decisions.

options.text: Only weak Wi-Fi signals
options.feedback: That is unrelated to the main idea here.

options.text: Only outdated hardware
options.feedback: Social engineering focuses on people first.

checkQuestions.prompt: What is the safest response to an urgent request from apparent authority?

options.text: Comply immediately to avoid trouble
options.feedback: That is the rushed response an attacker wants.

options.text: Verify through a trusted separate channel
options.feedback: Correct. Independent verification helps break the manipulation.

options.text: Assume it is safe if the tone sounds confident
options.feedback: Confident tone is easy to fake.
